Choosing a Bike Your Pillion Will Love

If you regularly tour with a pillion, the bike choice should consider their comfort as much as yours. A cramped, vibrating perch with minimal grab rails and no wind protection will ensure your pillion never wants to tour again. The best pillion bikes provide genuine rear comfort that makes two-up touring a pleasure for both rider and passenger.

What Makes a Good Pillion Bike?

  • Rear seat — Wide, well-padded, and at a comfortable height relative to the rider. The pillion should be able to see over the rider's shoulders without craning their neck.
  • Footpeg position — Low enough that the pillion's knees are not drawn up uncomfortably, but not so low that foot clearance in corners is compromised.
  • Grab handles — Solid, well-positioned handles that the pillion can grip without reaching awkwardly. A top box also provides a backrest.
  • Engine character — Smooth engines reduce vibration fatigue for the pillion. Inline fours and flat twins are typically smoother than singles and V-twins.
  • Suspension — Must handle the additional weight without wallowing. Adjustable or electronic suspension is a significant advantage for two-up riding.

Best Pillion Touring Bikes 2026

Honda Gold Wing — Nothing beats the Gold Wing for pillion luxury. The rear seat is a genuine armchair with heating, armrests, and an audio system. The flat-six engine is silk-smooth and the chassis handles two-up weight effortlessly. If pillion comfort is the top priority, this is the undisputed champion.

BMW R 1250 RT — The sport-touring Gold Wing rival. The boxer engine provides smooth, vibration-free power and the electrically adjustable screen protects both rider and pillion. The rear seat is elevated for pillion visibility and well-padded.

BMW R 1300 GS — The GS may look like a solo adventure bike but the elevated rear seat gives pillions an excellent view and comfortable perch. Electronic suspension adjusts automatically for two-up weight.

Yamaha FJR1300 — The sport-touring legend with an incredibly smooth inline four. The pillion seat is wide and well-positioned, and the built-in panniers keep luggage weight low and balanced.

Kawasaki Versys 1000 SE — The inline four is exceptionally smooth for pillion comfort. Good rear seat, effective grab handles, and electronic suspension that handles weight changes well.

Take your pillion bike shopping with you. Have them sit on every bike you are considering, in full gear, and assess the seat, pegs, and grab handles. Their opinion should carry equal weight in the decision — after all, they will be sitting on it for hundreds of miles.

Test Ride Together

Many dealers allow accompanied test rides with a pillion. Take advantage of this — a bike that feels perfect solo may feel completely different with a passenger. Pay attention to how the suspension handles the extra weight, whether the pillion can communicate comfortably, and how the bike steers with the changed weight distribution. faq.q: What makes a good pillion bike?
faq.a: Look for a wide, well-padded rear seat set high enough that the passenger can see over your shoulders, footpegs positioned so their knees are not drawn up uncomfortably, and solid grab handles or a top-box backrest. A smooth engine reduces vibration fatigue and suspension that copes with the extra weight prevents wallowing. Inline fours and flat twins are typically smoothest.

faq.q: Is the Honda Gold Wing really the best for pillions?
faq.a: For outright pillion luxury, yes. The Gold Wing's rear seat is a genuine armchair with heating, armrests and an audio system, the flat-six engine is exceptionally smooth, and the chassis carries two-up weight effortlessly. If passenger comfort is your top priority and budget allows, nothing else comes close, though it is large and heavy to manage at low speed.

faq.q: Should my pillion help choose the bike?
faq.a: Absolutely. The passenger will spend hundreds of miles on the rear seat, so their opinion should carry equal weight. Take them bike shopping, have them sit on every candidate in full gear, and assess the seat, pegs and grab handles together. Where possible, arrange an accompanied test ride, as a bike that feels great solo can feel very different two-up.

faq.q: Do I need electronic suspension for two-up touring?
faq.a: It is not essential but it is a real advantage. Electronic or semi-active suspension automatically adjusts preload and damping for the added pillion and luggage weight, keeping the handling composed without manual fiddling. On bikes with conventional suspension you can achieve similar results by manually increasing rear preload, but you must remember to reset it when riding solo again.
